```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}

# k-fold cross-validation schematic: one row per round, held-out fold shaded
draw_folds <- function(k = 5) {
  par(mar = c(1.5, 4.5, 0.5, 0.5))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, k), ylim = c(0, k), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (r in seq_len(k)) {
    for (f in seq_len(k)) {
      rect(f - 1, k - r, f - 0.05, k - r + 0.85,
           col = if (f == r) "steelblue" else "grey88", border = NA)
    }
    mtext(paste("round", r), side = 2, at = k - r + 0.42, las = 1, line = 0.3, cex = 0.8)
  }
  text(k / 2, -0.3, "blue = held out (scored), grey = used to fit", cex = 0.8, xpd = TRUE)
}
```

R code from this page is also in the
[companion script](lecture_notes/CODE_Week10_ModelComparison.R).
Packages: `emdbook`, `MASS`, `glmnet`, `cmdstanr`, `loo`.

This material follows Bolker, *Ecological Models and Data in R*,
section 6.6 (pp. 267-290).

# Likelihood ratio tests, AIC, and regularization {#frequentist}

How do we compare models that differ in complexity? This part covers
the most rigorous test (predicting new data), two shortcuts that need
only one fit (the likelihood ratio test and AIC), and regularization,
which keeps every covariate in a single model and shrinks the
coefficients toward 0.

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=150}
draw_workflow("COMPARE")
```

The FIT step gives estimates and their uncertainty for one model at a
time. COMPARE weighs models against each other. It has three parts:

1. Does the model fit the data at all?
2. Does it beat its rivals, including a null model, and predict new data?
3. Is it relevant to the problem we started with? (A judgment, not a
   statistic.)

Here we focus on part 2, comparing models fit to the same data. This
includes:

- **Null-model tests:** is there evidence that a model (a theory)
  outperforms an uninteresting one?
- **Model selection:** which of several alternative models is best
  supported by the data?
- **Multimodel inference:** when several models have some support,
  base predictions and inferences on all of them.

Adding parameters always improves the fit to the data in hand (see the
[WOD](#wod)), so in-sample fit can't answer these questions. The most
rigorous test is how well a model predicts new data from the same
process:

- **Validation:** fit the model to one data set and score its
  predictions on data it never saw, ideally collected separately.
- **Cross-validation:** without new data, hold out part of the data,
  fit to the rest, score the held-out part, and rotate. This means
  fitting the model many times. (More on this later in the course.)

Because cross-validation takes many refits, we often rely on shortcuts
that use a single fit to all the data:

- **LRT:** does a bigger (nested) model fit better than chance alone
  would explain?
- **AIC:** estimates how well a model would predict new data. In large
  samples it ranks models about the same way leave-one-out
  cross-validation does.

Ridge regression and the lasso take a third route: fit one large model
and penalize the size of its coefficients, usually choosing the penalty
strength by cross-validation.

Models that pass these tests are **corroborated**, not proven.

## 2. WOD: bias-variance tradeoff {#wod}

The WOD (a short warm-up exercise at the start of class) gave seven
measurements of seedling height and soil moisture, and two models: a
straight line and a curve through every point. Both models were used to
predict height at 19% moisture, where there were no data.

```{r wod, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=3.2}
wod_x <- c(3, 8, 10, 14, 25, 27, 32)
wod_y <- c(7, 8, 15, 9.5, 18, 16, 20.5)
wod_line <- lm(wod_y ~ wod_x)
wod_curve <- splinefun(wod_x, wod_y, method = "natural")
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 0.5))
plot(wod_x, wod_y, pch = 19, xlim = c(0, 35), ylim = c(0, 25), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
     xlab = "Soil moisture (%)", ylab = "Seedling height (cm)")
abline(v = 19, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
abline(wod_line, lwd = 2)
xs <- seq(2, 33, 0.1)
lines(xs, pmin(wod_curve(xs), 25), lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "steelblue")
points(19, 14, pch = 4, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2.5, col = "firebrick")
legend("topleft", c("straight line", "curve through every point", "new plot (19%, 14 cm)"),
       lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 4), col = c("black", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

- Sum of squared residuals: line `r f1(sum(resid(wod_line)^2))`, curve 0.
- The new plot measured 14 cm. The line predicted
  `r f1(predict(wod_line, data.frame(wod_x = 19)))`; this curve predicted
  `r f1(wod_curve(19))`.

A perfect fit to seven points says little about prediction. Suppose we
repeated the study many times with new seedlings from the same process,
refitting both models each time:

- A very flexible model fits the noise along with the signal. Its
  predictions are about right on average (low **bias**) but swing widely
  from one sample to the next (high **variance**).
- A very simple model, such as a constant mean height, gives nearly the
  same prediction from every sample, but it misses a real trend, so it
  is consistently wrong (high bias, low variance).

Prediction error on new data includes both. More complexity lowers bias
but raises variance, so the best predictive model lies somewhere between
the extremes.

In the figure below, the study is repeated 20 times. Each sample uses
the WOD's moisture values, with heights simulated from the red line plus
random noise.

```{r bias-variance, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
# 20 new samples from a straight-line truth at the WOD's moisture values
truth <- coef(wod_line)
noise_sd <- summary(wod_line)$sigma
set.seed(746)
sims <- replicate(20, truth[1] + truth[2] * wod_x + rnorm(length(wod_x), 0, noise_sd))
xs <- seq(2, 33, 0.25)
pred_line <- pred_curve <- numeric(20)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 35), ylim = c(0, 30), xlab = "Soil moisture (%)", ylab = "Height (cm)",
     main = "Straight line, 20 samples")
for (i in seq_len(20)) {
  fit <- lm(sims[, i] ~ wod_x)
  lines(xs, coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * xs, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.4))
  pred_line[i] <- coef(fit)[1] + coef(fit)[2] * 19
}
abline(truth, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 35), ylim = c(0, 30), xlab = "Soil moisture (%)", ylab = "Height (cm)",
     main = "Curve through every point, 20 samples")
for (i in seq_len(20)) {
  f <- splinefun(wod_x, sims[, i], method = "natural")
  lines(xs, f(xs), col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.5))
  pred_curve[i] <- f(19)
}
abline(truth, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
stripchart(list(line = pred_line, curve = pred_curve), method = "jitter", pch = 19,
           col = c("black", "steelblue"), vertical = TRUE,
           ylab = "Predicted height at 19% (cm)", main = "Predictions at 19%")
abline(h = truth[1] + truth[2] * 19, lwd = 3, col = "firebrick")
```

Both models center near the true height at 19% (red line), but the
curve's predictions vary more than twice as much (SD
`r f1(sd(pred_curve))` cm vs. `r f1(sd(pred_line))` cm for the line).

## 3. Likelihood ratio test

Bolker's balsam fir data (section 6.6): cone counts on 242 trees, some
at "wave" sites (where stands regenerate in waves) and some not. Model:
$\text{cones} \sim \text{NegBin}(\mu = a\,\text{DBH}^b, k)$. Do wave
sites differ?

- **Full model:** separate $a$, $b$, $k$ for wave and non-wave sites (6 parameters).
- **Reduced model:** one $a$, $b$, $k$ for all trees (3 parameters).

The likelihood ratio test is the oldest shortcut. It applies to
**nested** models, where the reduced model is the full model with some
parameters fixed (often at 0). Here the reduced model fixes three: wave
and non-wave sites share $a$, $b$, and $k$.

Since the full model always fits at least as well, the real question is
whether it fits better than extra parameters fitting pure noise would.
If the reduced model is true, then in large samples the deviance

$$D = 2(\text{NLL}_{\text{reduced}} - \text{NLL}_{\text{full}})$$

follows a $\chi^2_r$ distribution, where $r$ is the number of fixed
parameters (Wilks' theorem).

The test:

1. Fit both models by maximum likelihood and record each minimum NLL.
2. Compute $D$. It is never negative, since the full model fits at
   least as well.
3. Compare $D$ with the 95% quantile of $\chi^2_r$ (`qchisq(0.95, r)`).
4. If $D$ exceeds it ($p < 0.05$), the extra parameters improve the fit
   more than fitting noise usually would: evidence for the full model.
   Otherwise keep the reduced model, following the principle of
   parsimony.

The 1.92 cutoff for likelihood-based confidence intervals comes from the
same result with $r = 1$: $\chi^2_1$'s 95% quantile is 3.84, and
$3.84/2 = 1.92$ on the NLL scale.

```{r fir-data}
library(emdbook)
fir <- na.omit(FirDBHFec[, c("TOTCONES", "DBH", "WAVE_NON")])   # balsam fir, 242 trees
fir$TOTCONES <- round(fir$TOTCONES)
wave <- as.numeric(fir$WAVE_NON)   # 1 = non-wave, 2 = wave

plot(TOTCONES ~ DBH, data = fir, col = wave, pch = 19,
     xlab = "DBH (cm)", ylab = "Total cones")
legend("topleft", c("non-wave", "wave"), col = 1:2, pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

```{r fir-lrt}
# cones ~ NegBin(mu = a * DBH^b, size = k); a, b, k can be vectors (one value per tree)
nll_nb <- function(a, b, k) {
  -sum(dnbinom(fir$TOTCONES, mu = a * fir$DBH^b, size = k, log = TRUE))
}

# full model: separate a, b, k for wave and non-wave sites (6 parameters)
nll_full <- function(p) nll_nb(p[1:2][wave], p[3:4][wave], p[5:6][wave])
# no-wave model: one a, b, k for all trees (3 parameters)
nll_nowave <- function(p) nll_nb(p[1], p[2], p[3])

# Nelder-Mead to get close, then BFGS to polish
fit_model <- function(nll, start) {
  fit <- optim(start, nll, control = list(maxit = 10000))
  optim(fit$par, nll, method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 10000))
}
fit_full <- fit_model(nll_full, c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1))
fit_nowave <- fit_model(nll_nowave, c(1, 2, 1))
c(full = fit_full$value, nowave = fit_nowave$value)   # min NLL

# deviance = 2 * (NLL_reduced - NLL_full) ~ chi-square, df = difference in parameters
deviance <- 2 * (fit_nowave$value - fit_full$value)
deviance
qchisq(0.95, df = 3)                            # critical value
pchisq(deviance, df = 3, lower.tail = FALSE)    # p-value
```

```{r fir-chisq, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.5}
curve(dchisq(x, df = 3), 0, 12, lwd = 2, xlab = "Deviance", ylab = "Density",
      main = "Deviance under the reduced model (df = 3)")
abline(v = qchisq(0.95, 3), lty = 2)
abline(v = deviance, col = "red", lwd = 3)
```

With $D = `r f2(deviance)`$, well below the cutoff, we keep the no-wave
model.

```{r fir-poisson}
# Poisson, no wave effect (2 parameters)
nll_pois <- function(p) -sum(dpois(fir$TOTCONES, p[1] * fir$DBH^p[2], log = TRUE))
fit_pois <- fit_model(nll_pois, c(1, 2))
2 * (fit_pois$value - fit_nowave$value)
```

> **Question:** Is the Poisson model nested in the negative binomial? Can we
> use an LRT here?

Keeping the reduced model doesn't show that wave and non-wave trees
are alike. It shows that these 242 trees can't distinguish them.

## 4. AIC

$$\text{AIC} = -2\log\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta) + 2k$$

AIC can rank any set of models fit to the same response data, nested or
not. The $2k$ term estimates how much the in-sample fit overstates the
fit to new data (the problem in the [WOD](#wod)). The
[AIC penalty handout](lecture_notes/NOTES_Reference_AICPenalty.pdf)
shows where it comes from.

- $\Delta_i = \text{AIC}_i - \text{AIC}_{\min}$
- Akaike weights: $w_i = e^{-\Delta_i/2} / \sum_j e^{-\Delta_j/2}$
- AICc adds a small-sample correction; BIC uses $k \log n$ in place of
  $2k$ (a harsher penalty).

```{r fir-aic}
# two intermediate models: wave changes only a and k (5 parameters), or only b (4)
nll_constb <- function(p) nll_nb(p[1:2][wave], p[3], p[4:5][wave])
nll_constak <- function(p) nll_nb(p[1], p[2:3][wave], p[4])
fit_constb <- fit_model(nll_constb, c(1, 1, 2, 1, 1))
fit_constak <- fit_model(nll_constak, c(1, 2, 2, 1))

fits <- list(full = fit_full, const_b = fit_constb, const_ak = fit_constak,
             no_wave = fit_nowave, poisson = fit_pois)
n <- nrow(fir)
aic_tab <- data.frame(model = names(fits),
                      k = sapply(fits, function(f) length(f$par)),
                      nll = sapply(fits, function(f) f$value))
aic_tab$AIC <- 2 * aic_tab$nll + 2 * aic_tab$k                  # -2 log L + 2k
aic_tab$dAIC <- aic_tab$AIC - min(aic_tab$AIC)
aic_tab$weight <- exp(-aic_tab$dAIC / 2) / sum(exp(-aic_tab$dAIC / 2))
aic_tab$AICc <- aic_tab$AIC + 2 * aic_tab$k * (aic_tab$k + 1) / (n - aic_tab$k - 1)
aic_tab$BIC <- 2 * aic_tab$nll + log(n) * aic_tab$k             # -2 log L + k log(n)
aic_tab <- aic_tab[order(aic_tab$AIC), ]
rownames(aic_tab) <- NULL
```

```{r fir-aic-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(aic_tab, digits = 2)
w_nowave <- aic_tab$weight[aic_tab$model == "no_wave"]
```

> **Question:** The no-wave model has weight `r f2(w_nowave)`. Is there a
> `r round(100 * w_nowave)`% chance it's the true model?

Look at `const_ak`. It has one more parameter than the no-wave model and
an NLL only `r f2(fit_nowave$value - fit_constak$value)` lower, yet it
is just `r f2(aic_tab$dAIC[aic_tab$model == "const_ak"])` AIC units
behind. A useless parameter costs at most 2 AIC units, so being within
2 of the best model isn't evidence of support (Arnold 2010, *J. Wildl.
Manage.* 74: 1175-1178).

## 5. Regularization: ridge and LASSO {#regularization}

**Example: brown creepers.** Counts at 50 point-count stations, with 10
standardized habitat covariates. These data are simulated, so we know
the truth: only big trees, snags, and road distance matter.

Ten covariates give $2^{10} = 1024$ possible subsets. Instead of
searching them all, we can keep all 10 and penalize the size of the
coefficients:

$$\text{ridge: } \text{NLL}(\beta) + \lambda\sum_j \beta_j^2 \qquad\qquad
  \text{lasso: } \text{NLL}(\beta) + \lambda\sum_j |\beta_j|$$

AIC charges for each parameter; these penalties grow with the size of
the coefficients. One $\lambda$ applies to every coefficient, so the
covariates are standardized first. The lasso penalty has a corner at 0
that can set coefficients to exactly 0 (try the slider in
[Prices and budgets](#budgets)).

A penalty also makes the search simpler. Instead of comparing 1024
unordered models, we turn one dial: as $\lambda$ falls from large to 0,
the fit moves from the intercept alone to the full MLE, and
cross-validation only has to choose a point along that path. The path
passes through only a few of the 1024 subsets, in an order set by the
data, so it can miss the best one. In exchange, its estimates are
shrunk, and tuning one number overfits the held-out data less than
picking a winner from a thousand models.

```{r creeper-data}
library(MASS)
library(glmnet)

# brown creeper counts at 50 point-count stations, 10 standardized habitat covariates.
# Simulated, so we know the truth: only big_trees, snags, and road_dist matter.
covars <- c("canopy", "big_trees", "snags", "shrub", "elev", "slope",
            "north", "road_dist", "stream_dist", "grazing")
beta_true <- c(0, 0.5, 0.4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.3, 0, 0)
cov_mat <- diag(10)
cov_mat[1, 2] <- cov_mat[2, 1] <- 0.6    # canopy ~ big trees
cov_mat[1, 4] <- cov_mat[4, 1] <- -0.4   # canopy ~ shrub
cov_mat[5, 6] <- cov_mat[6, 5] <- 0.5    # elevation ~ slope
set.seed(19)
X <- mvrnorm(50, rep(0, 10), cov_mat)
colnames(X) <- covars
creepers <- rpois(50, exp(log(2) + X %*% beta_true))   # log(mu) = log(2) + X beta

# ordinary MLE with every covariate: no estimate is exactly 0
fit_glm <- glm(creepers ~ X, family = poisson)
round(coef(fit_glm)[-1], 2)
```

```{r creeper-subsets, cache=TRUE}
# all 2^10 = 1024 subsets, ranked by AIC
subsets <- expand.grid(rep(list(c(FALSE, TRUE)), 10))
subset_aic <- apply(subsets, 1, function(use) {
  if (!any(use)) return(AIC(glm(creepers ~ 1, family = poisson)))
  AIC(glm(creepers ~ X[, use, drop = FALSE], family = poisson))
})
covars[unlist(subsets[which.min(subset_aic), ])]   # best subset
sum(subset_aic - min(subset_aic) < 2)              # models within 2 AIC units

# AIC table of the top models: k counts the intercept
subset_tab <- data.frame(
  model = apply(subsets, 1, function(use) {
    if (!any(use)) "(intercept only)" else paste(covars[use], collapse = " + ")
  }),
  k = rowSums(subsets) + 1,
  AIC = subset_aic)
subset_tab$dAIC <- subset_tab$AIC - min(subset_tab$AIC)
subset_tab$weight <- exp(-subset_tab$dAIC / 2) / sum(exp(-subset_tab$dAIC / 2))
subset_tab <- subset_tab[order(subset_tab$AIC), ]
rownames(subset_tab) <- NULL
```

```{r creeper-subset-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(subset_tab[1:10, ], digits = 2)
```

> **Question:** Which covariates show up in nearly every top model? Which
> come and go?

```{r creeper-paths, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5}
# penalized NLL: NLL(beta) + lambda * sum(beta^2) (ridge) or lambda * sum(|beta|) (lasso)
fit_ridge <- glmnet(X, creepers, family = "poisson", alpha = 0)
fit_lasso <- glmnet(X, creepers, family = "poisson", alpha = 1)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit_ridge, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, main = "Ridge")
plot(fit_lasso, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, main = "Lasso")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

> **Question:** Read the lasso panel from right to left (from a big penalty
> to none). Which covariates enter first?

```{r creeper-cv}
# choose lambda by 10-fold cross-validation: predict each held-out tenth
set.seed(746)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(X, creepers, family = "poisson", alpha = 1)
plot(cv_lasso)   # left dashed line: lambda.min; right: lambda.1se (simplest within 1 SE)
coef_lasso <- coef(cv_lasso, s = "lambda.1se")[-1]

# same cross-validation for ridge (alpha = 0); same folds, so the two are comparable
set.seed(746)
cv_ridge <- cv.glmnet(X, creepers, family = "poisson", alpha = 0)
coef_ridge <- coef(cv_ridge, s = "lambda.1se")[-1]   # try s = "lambda.min": much less shrinkage

round(data.frame(truth = beta_true,
                 MLE = coef(fit_glm)[-1],
                 AIC_best = ifelse(unlist(subsets[which.min(subset_aic), ]), 1, 0),
                 ridge = coef_ridge,
                 lasso = coef_lasso,
                 row.names = covars), 2)
```

> **Question:** The lasso kept road distance but estimates its effect at
> `r f2(coef_lasso[8])`; the truth is 0.3. Is the lasso broken?

Neither AIC nor the lasso reliably recovers the true model. In 40
simulated data sets like this one, the AIC-best subset matched the true
set of covariates 12 times and the lasso 13 times.

## Discussion

**Q1.** AIC's best creeper model kept northness (several models within 2
units, top weight small); the lasso dropped it. Which covariates would
you report as "important," and how would you word it?

**Q2.** In a real survey, the lasso sets grazing to exactly 0. A manager
concludes that expanding grazing won't affect creepers. Do you agree?

# Prices, budgets, and cross-validation {#lab-tools}

These tools come up in a lab on Bd infection in frogs, which fits a
logistic model to a 60-pond survey with 8 pond features
([data](data/BdRegionalSurvey.csv)). This part offers another way to
picture regularization, as a price or a budget for coefficient size, along with
tips for `glmnet` and an outline of how cross-validation picks the
penalty.

## Prices and budgets {#budgets}

Think of fitting a model as shopping, with fit as the currency
(measured in NLL units). Coefficient size buys a lower NLL: the first
bit of a useful coefficient buys a lot, and later bits buy less. A
penalty restrains the spending in one of two equivalent ways.

**A price.** The penalized form, which is what `glmnet` computes:

$$\min_\beta \; \text{NLL}(\beta) + \lambda \cdot \text{size}(\beta),
  \qquad \text{size} = \sum_j \beta_j^2 \text{ (ridge) or } \sum_j |\beta_j| \text{ (lasso)}$$

- $\lambda$ is the price of coefficient size, paid in NLL units.
- There is no spending limit. The fit keeps adding size as long as the
  next unit lowers the NLL by more than it costs, and stops where the
  two balance.
- How much gets spent depends on the data: if the fit improves steeply,
  it pays for a lot of size even at a high price.
- At $\lambda = 0$, size is free and we get the MLE.

**A budget.** The constrained form:

$$\min_\beta \; \text{NLL}(\beta) \quad \text{subject to} \quad
  \sum_j \beta_j^2 \le t^2 \text{ (ridge) or } \sum_j |\beta_j| \le t \text{ (lasso)}$$

- $t$ is a fixed allowance of coefficient size, with no price. The fit
  spends it wherever it lowers the NLL most.
- If the MLE fits within the allowance, the limit doesn't bind and we
  get the MLE. Any $t$ at least as large as the MLE's size acts like an
  unlimited budget.

**The bridge.** Every price has a matching budget that gives the same
coefficients.

- Fix $\lambda$, fit, and add up the size of what was bought. That total
  is the matching $t$. (If some point within that budget had a lower
  NLL, its penalized total would be lower too, so the penalized fit
  couldn't have been the best.)
- Going the other way, the price that matches a budget $t$ is how much
  NLL one more unit of budget would buy.
- As $\lambda$ rises from 0, the matching $t$ shrinks from the size of
  the MLE toward 0. In practice we tune $\lambda$ (usually by
  cross-validation); $t$ pictures how much the fit ended up spending.

**Two price schedules.**

- Lasso: a flat price. Each unit of $|\beta_j|$ costs $\lambda$,
  starting with the first.
- Ridge: a rising price. Size costs $\lambda\beta_j^2$, so the next unit
  costs $2\lambda\beta_j$: almost nothing near 0, more the more you've
  already bought.

**One coefficient.** Take $\text{NLL}(\beta) = (\beta - 0.4)^2$, so the
MLE is 0.4. Raising $\beta$ from $b$ lowers the NLL at a rate of
$2(0.4 - b)$ per unit: 0.8 at $b = 0$, falling to 0 at the MLE.

- Lasso: buy until the rate equals the price, $2(0.4 - b) = \lambda$,
  so $\hat\beta = 0.4 - \lambda/2$ (for $\lambda < 0.8$). At
  $\lambda = 0.4$, $\hat\beta = 0.2$.
- Ridge: buy until the rate equals the next unit's price,
  $2(0.4 - b) = 2\lambda b$, so $\hat\beta = 0.4/(1 + \lambda)$. At
  $\lambda = 1$, $\hat\beta = 0.2$.
- Both match a budget of $t = 0.2$: given an allowance of 0.2 and no
  price, either penalty would buy the same $\hat\beta$.

Drag the slider. The left panel shows the lasso objective, with a dot at
its minimum; the right panel tracks the lasso and ridge estimates as
$\lambda$ increases.

```{r widget-lasso, echo=FALSE}
widget("lasso_kink.html")
```

> **Question:** Why does the lasso buy nothing at all once
> $\lambda \ge 0.8$, while ridge always buys some?

## Tools for the lab

- `glmnet(X, y, family = "binomial", alpha = )`: `alpha = 0` is ridge,
  `alpha = 1` (the default) is lasso.
- For binomial counts, `y = cbind(failures, successes)`, the reverse of
  `glm()`'s order.
- `glmnet` scales the NLL by the sample size, so its $\lambda$ isn't the
  $\lambda$ in a penalty you code by hand. Compare coefficients, not
  $\lambda$ values.

## Cross-validation

```{r folds, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5.5, fig.height=2.8}
draw_folds()
```

- Fit to 4/5 of the data, score the held-out 1/5 by its NLL, and rotate
  through all five folds.
- Choose the $\lambda$ with the best total held-out score. `lambda.1se`
  is the largest $\lambda$ (the simplest model) whose score is within one
  SE of the best.
- Each held-out fold plays the role of the new plot in the [WOD](#wod).
- Folds are random, so set a seed to reproduce them.

## Bonus: elastic net {#elastic-net}

The elastic net charges both prices at once, mixed by a second tuning
parameter $\alpha$ between 0 and 1:

$$\min_\beta \; \text{NLL}(\beta) + \lambda \sum_j \Big[\alpha|\beta_j| + (1 - \alpha)\beta_j^2\Big]$$

- $\lambda$ sets the overall price; $\alpha$ sets the mix. $\alpha = 1$ is
  the lasso and $\alpha = 0$ is ridge.
- The next unit of $|\beta_j|$ costs $\lambda\alpha + 2\lambda(1 - \alpha)|\beta_j|$:
  a flat fee from the lasso part, plus a rising price from the ridge
  part.
- The flat fee means a coefficient can still be exactly 0. The rising
  part keeps any one coefficient from getting large, so the fit spreads
  its spending more evenly than the lasso does.

For the [one-coefficient example](#budgets), buying until the NLL's rate
equals the price gives

$$\hat\beta = \frac{\max(0,\; 0.4 - \lambda\alpha/2)}{1 + \lambda(1 - \alpha)}.$$

The numerator is the lasso's threshold, now reached at
$\lambda = 0.8/\alpha$; the denominator is ridge's proportional
shrinkage, applied on top.

In the left panel, the purple line is the price of the next unit and
the grey line is what it buys; the estimate sits where they cross, or at
0 if the first unit already costs more than it's worth. Try $\alpha = 1$
and $\alpha = 0$ to recover the [slider above](#budgets), then values in
between.

```{r widget-elastic-net, echo=FALSE}
widget("elastic_net.html")
```

In `glmnet`, the `alpha` argument is this mix. Its ridge term is
written $\frac{1 - \alpha}{2}\beta_j^2$, half of the one here, so its
$\lambda$ values won't match a hand calculation. `cv.glmnet()` tunes
$\lambda$ only. To choose $\alpha$, run it at a few values of `alpha`
with the same `foldid` and compare the cross-validation scores. The
elastic net is a common default when there are many predictors,
especially correlated ones, where the lasso and ridge behave
differently; the Bd lab works through how.

# Bayesian model comparison and shrinkage priors {#bayesian}

This part brings the same ideas to models fit by MCMC. A ridge penalty
is equivalent to a Normal prior, so regularization has a direct Bayesian
counterpart. WAIC and LOO estimate predictive performance from the
posterior, and shrinkage priors do the job of ridge and the lasso while
keeping the full posterior uncertainty.

## 1. Why not AIC?

AIC needs a single best-fit $\hat\theta$ and a count of parameters. An
MCMC fit gives a whole posterior instead, and priors constrain
parameters to different degrees, so the parameter count is no longer
clear-cut. WAIC and LOO (section 3) handle both problems.

## 2. Ridge is a prior

Eight survey routes each report a change in log abundance,
$y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma = 0.15)$, where $\mu$ is the
regional trend.

1. The ridge fit from [Regularization](#regularization), with one parameter:
   $$\text{PNLL}(\mu) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \lambda \mu^2$$
   (the NLL is the Normal density's exponent; the
   $\log\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}$ terms don't involve $\mu$, so they drop out).
2. Bayes' rule, then $-\log$:
   $$P(\mu \mid y) \propto \mathcal{L}(\mu)\, P(\mu)
     \quad\Rightarrow\quad
     -\log P(\mu \mid y) = -\log \mathcal{L}(\mu) - \log P(\mu) + \text{const.}$$
3. A skeptical prior centered on "no trend," $\mu \sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau)$:
   $$-\log P(\mu) = \frac{\mu^2}{2\tau^2} + \text{const.}$$
4. Together:
   $$-\log P(\mu \mid y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu^2}{2\tau^2} + \text{const.}$$
5. This matches the ridge PNLL when $\lambda = 1/(2\tau^2)$, so both
   have the same minimum: **the ridge estimate is the posterior mode.**
   A narrow prior means a big penalty; a vague prior
   ($\tau \to \infty$) gives $\lambda \to 0$, the MLE.
6. Setting the derivative to 0:
   $$\hat\mu = \bar y \cdot \frac{n}{n + \sigma^2/\tau^2}$$
   This is the MLE times a shrinkage factor below 1. The prior acts like
   $\sigma^2/\tau^2$ extra routes that each reported exactly 0.

```{r ridge-prior}
# 8 survey routes: change in log abundance ~ Normal(mu, sigma = 0.15); mu = regional trend
route_y <- c(0.12, -0.05, 0.20, 0.08, -0.10, 0.15, 0.02, 0.10)
sigma <- 0.15
tau <- 0.05                       # prior: mu ~ Normal(0, tau)
lambda <- 1 / (2 * tau^2)         # ridge penalty that matches it
nll_mu <- function(mu) sapply(mu, function(m) sum((route_y - m)^2) / (2 * sigma^2))
pnll_mu <- function(mu) nll_mu(mu) + lambda * mu^2                       # ridge
neg_log_post <- function(mu) nll_mu(mu) - dnorm(mu, 0, tau, log = TRUE)  # Bayes
c(MLE = mean(route_y),
  ridge = optimize(pnll_mu, c(-1, 1))$minimum,
  posterior_mode = optimize(neg_log_post, c(-1, 1))$minimum)
```

Drag the prior SD $\tau$. The posterior, and the ridge $\lambda$ that
matches it, shift between the data and 0.

```{r widget-ridge-prior, echo=FALSE}
widget("ridge_prior.html")
```

> **Question:** Which prior matches the lasso penalty, $\lambda|\mu|$?

## 3. WAIC and LOO

- **Score:** the expected log predictive density (elpd). For each data
  point, average its likelihood over the posterior draws, take the log,
  and sum over points. Higher is better; the "IC" versions are
  $-2 \times$ elpd.
- **Penalty:** effective number of parameters, estimated from the posterior.
  - DIC (Bolker 6.6.3): $p_D$ = mean deviance minus the deviance at the posterior means.
  - WAIC: $p_{\text{waic}}$ = the summed posterior variance of each point's log likelihood.
  - LOO: approximates refitting the model without each point (PSIS).
    Pareto $k > 0.7$ flags points where the approximation fails.
- Stan has to save `log_lik[i]` for every observation, in `generated quantities`.

```{r fir-stan, cache=TRUE, results="hide", echo=-10}
library(cmdstanr)
library(loo)

# fir NegBin power law; G = 1: one a, b, k for all trees; G = 2: separate for wave/non-wave
fir_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> G;
  array[N] int<lower=0> cones;
  vector<lower=0>[N] dbh;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=G> grp;
}
parameters {
  vector[G] log_a;
  vector[G] b;
  vector<lower=0>[G] k;
}
model {
  log_a ~ normal(0, 5);
  b ~ normal(0, 5);
  k ~ exponential(0.1);
  cones ~ neg_binomial_2(exp(log_a[grp]) .* pow(dbh, b[grp]), k[grp]);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;    // one value per tree, for WAIC and LOO
  for (i in 1:N)
    log_lik[i] = neg_binomial_2_lpmf(cones[i] | exp(log_a[grp[i]]) * dbh[i]^b[grp[i]], k[grp[i]]);
}
"
fir_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(fir_code))
fit_fir <- function(G) {
  grp <- if (G == 1) rep(1L, nrow(fir)) else wave
  fir_model$sample(data = list(N = nrow(fir), G = G, cones = fir$TOTCONES, dbh = fir$DBH,
                               grp = grp),
                   chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0,
                   show_messages = FALSE)
}
fit_nowave_b <- fit_fir(1)
fit_full_b <- fit_fir(2)
for (f in list(fit_nowave_b, fit_full_b)) f$draws()   # read draws into memory so the knitr cache keeps them
```

```{r fir-ic, cache=TRUE, dependson="fir-stan"}
# DIC (Bolker 6.6.3): pD = mean deviance - deviance at posterior means; DIC = Dhat + 2 pD
dic <- function(fit, G) {
  grp <- if (G == 1) rep(1L, nrow(fir)) else wave
  d_bar <- mean(-2 * rowSums(fit$draws("log_lik", format = "matrix")))
  pm <- function(v) colMeans(fit$draws(v, format = "matrix"))
  d_hat <- -2 * sum(dnbinom(fir$TOTCONES, mu = exp(pm("log_a")[grp]) * fir$DBH^pm("b")[grp],
                            size = pm("k")[grp], log = TRUE))
  c(DIC = d_hat + 2 * (d_bar - d_hat), pD = d_bar - d_hat)
}
waic_nowave <- waic(fit_nowave_b$draws("log_lik", format = "matrix"))
waic_full <- waic(fit_full_b$draws("log_lik", format = "matrix"))
loo_nowave <- fit_nowave_b$loo()
loo_full <- fit_full_b$loo()
loo_nowave    # elpd_loo, p_loo, looic, and the Pareto k check

# the same two models, four ways (lower is better; penalties: k, pD, p_waic, p_loo)
ic_tab <- rbind(
  AIC = aic_tab$AIC[match(c("no_wave", "full"), aic_tab$model)],
  DIC = c(dic(fit_nowave_b, 1)["DIC"], dic(fit_full_b, 2)["DIC"]),
  WAIC = c(waic_nowave$estimates["waic", 1], waic_full$estimates["waic", 1]),
  LOOIC = c(loo_nowave$estimates["looic", 1], loo_full$estimates["looic", 1]))
colnames(ic_tab) <- c("no_wave", "full")
round(ic_tab, 1)
fir_comp <- loo_compare(list(no_wave = loo_nowave, full = loo_full))
fir_comp
```

> **Question:** The full model is `r f1(-fir_comp["full", "elpd_diff"])`
> elpd behind, SE `r f1(fir_comp["full", "se_diff"])`. What can you
> conclude?

Unlike AIC, LOO gives a standard error for the difference between two
models.

## 4. Shrinkage priors {#shrinkage}

The prior's scale plays the role of $\lambda$: a Normal prior on the
slopes corresponds to ridge, a Laplace prior to the lasso. Here are the
brown creepers from [Regularization](#regularization) again, with three
different priors on the 10 slopes:

```{r creeper-stan, cache=TRUE, results="hide", echo=-6}
# creepers again: Poisson regression; prior on the slopes is Normal(0, s) or Laplace(0, s)
pois_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N, K] X;
  array[N] int<lower=0> y;
  int<lower=1, upper=2> prior;    // 1 = Normal, 2 = Laplace
  real<lower=0> s;
}
parameters {
  real b0;
  vector[K] beta;
}
model {
  b0 ~ normal(0, 5);
  if (prior == 1) beta ~ normal(0, s);
  else beta ~ double_exponential(0, s);
  y ~ poisson_log(b0 + X * beta);
}
generated quantities {
  vector[N] log_lik;
  for (i in 1:N) log_lik[i] = poisson_log_lpmf(y[i] | b0 + X[i] * beta);
}
"
pois_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(pois_code))
fit_creepers <- function(prior, s) {
  pois_model$sample(data = list(N = 50, K = 10, X = X, y = creepers, prior = prior, s = s),
                    chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0,
                    show_messages = FALSE)
}
fits_shrink <- list(vague = fit_creepers(1, 10), normal = fit_creepers(1, 0.2),
                    laplace = fit_creepers(2, 0.15))
for (f in fits_shrink) f$draws()   # read draws into memory so the knitr cache keeps them
```

```{r creeper-intervals, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5, dependson="creeper-stan"}
# posterior medians and 90% intervals for each slope, under each prior; x = truth
post_sum <- lapply(fits_shrink, function(f) {
  as.matrix(f$summary("beta", "median", ~quantile(.x, c(0.05, 0.95)))[, -1])
})
par(mar = c(4, 7, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(-0.5, 1), ylim = c(0.5, 10.5), yaxt = "n", xlab = "Slope (per SD)", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = 10:1, labels = covars, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
abline(v = 0, col = "grey70")
offsets <- c(vague = 0.25, normal = 0, laplace = -0.25)
for (p in names(post_sum)) {
  yy <- (10:1) + offsets[p]
  segments(post_sum[[p]][, 2], yy, post_sum[[p]][, 3], yy, lwd = 2, col = match(p, names(post_sum)))
  points(post_sum[[p]][, 1], yy, pch = 19, col = match(p, names(post_sum)))
}
points(beta_true, 10:1, pch = 4, cex = 1.3, lwd = 2)
points(coef_lasso, 10:1, pch = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("vague prior", "Normal(0, 0.2)", "Laplace(0, 0.15)", "truth", "glmnet lasso"),
       col = c(1:3, 1, 1), pch = c(19, 19, 19, 4, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

```{r creeper-loo, cache=TRUE, dependson="creeper-stan"}
sapply(fits_shrink, function(f) f$loo()$estimates["p_loo", 1])   # effective parameters shrink
loo_compare(lapply(fits_shrink, function(f) f$loo()))
```

```{r north-numbers, echo=FALSE}
north_lap <- post_sum$laplace[7, ]
```

> **Question:** The cross-validated lasso in
> [Regularization](#regularization) set northness to exactly 0. The Laplace
> posterior says `r f2(north_lap[1])` (90% interval `r f2(north_lap[2])`
> to `r f2(north_lap[3])`). Which is more honest?

**Horseshoe prior** (sketch only): a taller spike at 0 plus heavier
tails, so small effects shrink hard and large ones barely shrink.

```{r prior-shapes, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.8}
# prior shapes: Normal, Laplace, horseshoe (simulated: Normal with half-Cauchy scale)
set.seed(746)
hs <- rnorm(1e6, 0, 0.1 * abs(rcauchy(1e6)))
curve(dnorm(x, 0, 0.2), -1, 1, n = 501, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 6), xlab = "Slope", ylab = "Prior density")
curve(dexp(abs(x), 1 / 0.15) / 2, -1, 1, n = 501, add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = 3)
lines(density(hs[abs(hs) < 1], bw = 0.01, n = 1024), lwd = 2, col = 4)
legend("topright", c("Normal (ridge)", "Laplace (lasso)", "horseshoe"), col = c(1, 3, 4),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

Choosing the prior scale amounts to choosing $\lambda$. Scales can be
compared by LOO, or the scale can be estimated from the data with a
hierarchical prior (covered later in the course).

## Discussion

**Q1.** LOO prefers the no-wave fir model by
`r f1(-fir_comp["full", "elpd_diff"])` elpd (SE
`r f1(fir_comp["full", "se_diff"])`). A colleague writes "wave
regeneration has no effect on cone production." Do you agree?

**Q2.** With a Laplace prior, northness gets a posterior median of
`r f2(north_lap[1])`; the cross-validated lasso said exactly 0. Which
would you report, and why?

## Bonus: Bayes factors and RJMCMC

- A **Bayes factor** is a ratio of marginal likelihoods (the likelihood
  averaged over the prior). It is sensitive to vague priors and hard to
  compute (Bolker 6.6.3).
- **RJMCMC and spike-and-slab** priors let the sampler jump between
  models, giving posterior model probabilities. They need discrete
  parameters, so they run in JAGS or NIMBLE rather than Stan.
